Let  

\[
AB=200,\qquad AC=225,\qquad BC=a .
\]

Denote the angle–bisector \(AD\) meeting \(BC\) at \(D\).  
By the Angle–Bisector Theorem

\[
\frac{BD}{CD}= \frac{AB}{AC}= \frac{200}{225}= \frac{8}{9}
\]

so we may write  

\[
BD=8k,\qquad CD=9k,\qquad BC=17k          \tag{1}
\]

for some positive integer \(k\).

---

### Power of a point

The circle \(\omega\) passes through \(A\) and is tangent to \(BC\) at \(D\).  
Hence for point \(B\),

\[
\text{pow}_\omega(B)=BD^2=AB\cdot BE .
\]

Since \(BE = AB-AE\), writing \(AE=s\) gives  

\[
200\,(200-s)=(8k)^2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad s=200-\frac{8}{25}k^2 .\tag{2}
\]

Similarly for point \(C\) with \(AF=t\),

\[
225\,(225-t)=(9k)^2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad t=225-\frac{9}{25}k^2 .\tag{3}
\]

Thus \(AE,AF\) are integers exactly when \(\frac{8}{25}k^2\) and \(\frac{9}{25}k^2\) are integers; i.e. \(k\) must be a multiple of \(5\).

Write \(k=5m\;(m\in\mathbb Z_{>0})\). Then (2) and (3) become  

\[
AE=s = 200-8m^2,\qquad AF=t = 225-9m^2 .
\]

Because \(AE,AF>0\),

\[
200-8m^2>0,\qquad 225-9m^2>0\Longrightarrow m^2<25\Longrightarrow m=1,2,3,4 .
\]

Hence  

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
m & AE & AF & BC=17k=85m \\ \hline
1 & 192 & 216 & 85 \\ 
2 & 168 & 189 & 170 \\ 
3 & 128 & 144 & 255 \\ 
4 &  72 &  81 & 340 
\end{array}
\]

All four triples give integer \(AE,AF,BD=40m,CD=45m\) and satisfy the required geometric condition (the circle meets segments \(AB,AC\) between \(A\) and the endpoints).

Thus the possible lengths of \(BC\) are  

\[
85,\;170,\;255,\;340 .
\]

Their sum is  

\[
85+170+255+340 = 850 .
\]

\[
\boxed{850}
\]
